21.17.6.en: God layeth up his iniquity for his children:

21.18.0.en: he rewardeth him, and he shall know it [19].

21.18.1.en: At times God lets the wicked prosper, but they bequeath failure to their offspring. So the sons inherit, with the wealth that arose from injustice and iniquity, the curse and destruction.

21.18.2.en: Perhaps some ask: What is the fault of the sons that they should inherit from their fathers grievous evils?

21.18.3.en: First: God is not unjust, and does not punish sons for the evils of their fathers. For the soul that sinneth, it shall die. Rather, God wanted the fathers' repentance, that they might lay up divine righteousness for their children. We do not deny the effect of the fathers' lives on their children, but the children of some of the wicked were saints, and the crowns of their sons became great, because they did not fill up the measure of their fathers in evil, but received God as their Father, walking by His Holy Spirit. And there were also wicked sons of holy fathers, so that the holiness of their fathers' life became a cause of greater judgment.

21.18.4.en: Second: God threatens the wicked with what will befall their children because of their evils, for often a man cares little about what will befall himself, but grieves intensely over what befalls his children. As though the aim of this threat is the repentance of the fathers for fear of the destruction of their children.

21.18.5.en: * We know that it is written: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation" (Ex 34:7). And it is also written: "What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord GOD, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek 18:2-4). Thus in these two passages, despite the difference in meaning, the mind of the hearer must learn to search with the utmost care the way of discernment. We have inherited ancestral sin from our parents, and if we are not released from it by the grace of baptism, we carry with us the very sins of our fathers, seeing that we are still one with them...

21.18.6.en: In any case this can be understood in another way also: that whoever imitates the way of evil of his wicked father is bound to his sins also. But he who does not follow his father's evil will not bear the weight of his disobedience. Thus the wicked son of a wicked father is bound not only to the sins that he himself added, but also to the sins of his father, since he practiced his father's evil works, which he knows God is angry at. Since he did not fear to add to them his own evils... Therefore it is rightly said: [unto the third and fourth generation]. For up to the third and fourth generation the children can witness the lives of their fathers and imitate them, so that vengeance extends even to those who witness what they imitate to their harm.

21.19.0.en: His eyes shall see his destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty [20].

21.19.1.en: The wicked man has deliberately closed his eyes so as not to see God's grace, and his insight was not opened to God's mercies, so he filled his cup with his rebellion and disobedience.

21.19.2.en: Often the wicked man shuts his eyes to what will befall him or his offspring because of his evils, but surely he will open his eyes on the day of the Lord to see his eternal destruction come upon him. He will drink of the wrath of the Almighty. This is the portion of his cup that he filled in the days of his sojourn in the world.

21.19.3.en: * If man, while in this life, wished to open his eyes to his sin, he would not afterwards [drink of the wrath of the Almighty]. But whoever turns his eyes away here from seeing his iniquity cannot avoid the sentence of judgment.

21.19.5.en: God calls us by every means to enjoy the illumination of the Holy Spirit, that our eyes may be opened to see the evils that have corrupted our being, at the same time as we enjoy seeing God's surpassing work for the forgiveness of our sins and for the enjoyment of union with Him.

21.19.6.en: If we see our destruction while we are still in this world, we flee to God Himself, who alone is able to keep us from the eternal wrath. But he who does not want to realize the truth of his evils fills his cup with divine wrath, to drink of it on the great day of the Lord.

21.20.0.en: For what pleasure hath he in his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off in the midst? [21]

21.20.1.en: Though Job has dwelt at length on the prosperity and success of some of the wicked, he makes clear what this success is, even if it extends through all the days of the wicked man's life, which are but a few months, so that he opens his eyes suddenly and finds himself falling under divine wrath.

21.20.2.en: In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, the Lord Christ showed us how he was troubled for his household while in Hades when he realized that all the good things he enjoyed in the days of his life on earth were unable to moisten his tongue. And his sorrow was doubled as he realized that his five brothers would follow him (Lk 16:25-28).

21.20.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the wicked man does not forget his house even in the world to come, for the Lord Himself told us of the rich man who lifted up his eyes in Hades asking for his five brothers (Lk 16:28). But this request no longer benefits his household, since the opportunity was lost to him.

21.20.4.en: Our work, as bearers of the Lord Jesus, the Fountain of joy, within us, is to rejoice and exult and be a cause of delight to our households. For if we rejoice here in our Christ who dwells in us, heaven rejoices in us, and many rejoice, so that we are as members of an almost heavenly family whose mark is true joy. Then even when we depart from the world we do not cease to ask for the delight of our households. This is what we touch in practice where we see saints in Paradise interceding for the joy of the whole world through its return to God and its enjoyment of divine joy.

21.21.0.en: 22 Shall any teach God knowledge? seeing he judgeth those that are high. 23 One dieth in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet. 24 His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow. 25 And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure. 26 They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them.

21.21.1.en: Shall any teach God knowledge? seeing he judgeth those that are high? [22]

21.21.2.en: No man can comprehend the knowledge of God, Judge of heaven and earth, who will judge the fallen angels and men on the day of judgment. His judgments are unsearchable and His ways past finding out. He alone decides whether a certain wicked man prospers here, even if his prosperity extends through all the days of his life, or fails. By His divine wisdom He directs what no man can comprehend. Since we are unable to comprehend God's knowledge, wisdom and plan, it is not for us to judge a person as righteous or wicked by what befalls him of troubles or what he enjoys of temporal blessings. Instead of judging our brethren, let us love them and pray for them for their spiritual edification and growth, and also for their repentance, that God may grant us with them true repentance and genuine spiritual growth.

21.21.3.en: *The judgments of God the Almighty upon us are exceedingly hidden and are not unjust. But when we lift the eyes of our minds to the heavenly things we see with our (inner) eyes that we have nothing to complain of regarding justice. For God the Almighty distinguishes the merits of the angels; some of them He established to dwell in eternal light without falling, while the others fell by their own will from steadfastness in their height, and descended to the wrath of eternal judgment... He does wonderful things above our level, and it is certainly clear that He orders all that concerns us with knowledge.

21.21.5.en: One dieth in his full strength,

21.22.0.en: being wholly at ease and quiet [23].

21.22.1.en: God alone determines whether a man dies in temporal peace and vain glory despite his persistence in his sins, and another dies in bitter pains and misery and wretchedness, though both meet together in the outer darkness.

21.22.2.en: A wicked man may die in his full strength, or in the fullness of his power, his strength not weakened by sickness or old age, "wholly at ease and quiet." In his entirety he is in rest and peace, not fearing death because he does not think of it or await it.

21.22.3.en: The Word of God came incarnate and dwelt among us to give us His true peace and the earnest of the glory He prepared for us from the foundation of the world. This peace and this glory alone satisfy the soul. But the false peace of the world and its vain glory deceive man, but only for a moment, and then pass away.

21.22.4.en: Here it behooves us to ask for the illumination of the Holy Spirit so that we may distinguish the kind of peace we are in, for there are many kinds of peace.

21.22.5.en: A. The peace that deceives the wicked, who drink iniquity like water, and in recklessness say: There is no God, no judgment and no eternity. [Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die] (1 Cor 15:32).

21.22.6.en: B. The peace that springs from friendships and sharing with others, such as our sharing with our loved ones in their joyful and sorrowful occasions, but we are not concerned with the salvation of their souls and ours. This peace is temporary. Of this peace the Lord Christ says: "Peace I leave with you" (Jn 14:27). As though He says: This peace of yours I do not take away from you, but leave it to you that it may be sanctified by My peace which I give you.

21.22.7.en: C. The divine peace which the Lord Christ promised us: [My peace I give unto you] (Jn 14:27). This peace, which is a divine gift, we enjoy through our fellowship with Him, His dwelling in our midst, and His constant accompaniment throughout the journey of our life. [Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world] (Mt 28:20).

21.23.0.en: His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow [24].

21.23.1.en: Some translate it "his breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moist with marrow." And in the Jesuits' translation it is "fatness clothes his forehead, and waters the marrow of his bones." Meaning that he is in good health, strong in build, caring for nothing but to live long years in joy and gladness. His hopes are broad in this life until death surprises him suddenly! Perhaps they defy death within them, as though it were not their portion.

21.23.2.en: Job's friends look at him as a man who has lost all he possessed of wealth and honor, and count this a sure sign of his wickedness, thinking he is in severe inward want and an emptiness that will not be filled. But he sees many wicked who are rich and possessed of authority and temporal honor, who reckon their breasts (udders) full of milk, that is, like a mother with a nursing infant in her arms offering him of her milk, and that their bones are full of vitality that dryness will never reach. These feelings that control such wicked men come from temporary wealth and vain honor, but only for a moment, when the Judge comes and they discover that they were in a dream that has vanished.

21.23.3.en: How great the difference between the milk that comes from temporary wealth and the bones that seem full of strength and vitality because of temporal honor, and the pure milk that God offers to His children, where they nurse souls with the life-giving word of God, and with the strong bones that God's grace provides, so that the believer is like the firm rock that the winds of this world will not shake!

21.23.4.en: * [His bowels are full of fatness, and his bones are moistened with marrow] [24]. For as fatness arises from an abundance of food, so pride arises from an overflow of good things, which makes the mind fat with abundance of riches, while his spirit is in arrogance...

21.24.0.en: There are people who have no wealth in this world, but desire it, and seek to be glorified, though unable to obtain in this world what they desire. While they have no substance (wealth) or honor to support them, by their evil lusts their conscience declares their guilt in the eyes of the Judge... Observe how for the same reason the rich man rejoices with an arrogant heart. Therefore it was rightly said: [They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them] [26].

21.24.1.en: But the blessed Job did not become proud when he had wealth, nor did he anxiously desire it when it was taken from him, nor did he perish through the external losses.

21.24.3.en: And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure [25].

21.24.4.en: Another dies after bitter pains and a wretched state, and meets him who spent the moment of his passing through this world in wealth and temporal glories. Neither wealth nor glory, nor pain either, can rescue the wicked on that day, so long as they have not returned to the Lord.

21.24.5.en: If God has allowed some of the wicked temporal blessings until their last breath in this world, it is that they might offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Giver of gifts, and return to Him, and enjoy fellowship with Him. And if He allows others sufferings, it is that their souls might not cling to the love of temporal things but long to pass over to God, and enjoy the glory He prepared for those who love Him. But alas, many do not profit by the gifts and do not learn by the sufferings!

21.24.6.en: As for God's children, temporal blessings support them in offering unceasing sacrifices of thanksgiving, and sufferings prove them in their receiving them as a fellowship of sufferings with their Savior.

21.24.7.en: They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them [26].

21.24.8.en: In the grave the healthy meet the sick, and the rich the poor; if one wicked man dies in a palace and another in a hut, they meet together with the company of the dead, and their portion is the fruit of their wickedness, the worm that dieth not and the fire that is not quenched.

21.25.0.en: *The mirth of the wicked passes into woe, and the woe of the righteous soul passes from sorrow to joy. Thus wealth ought not to lift up the soul, nor poverty to confound it. The blessed Job did not receive harmful thoughts in the midst of material losses, but those who despised him under the stroke of the rod he rebuked, saying: "Behold, I know your thoughts..." [27].

21.25.1.en: * How can external losses harm him who has not lost that One (God) whom he loved within him?

21.26.0.en: 27 Behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me. 28 For ye say, Where is the house of the prince? and where are the dwelling places of the wicked? 29 Have ye not asked them that go by the way? and do ye not know their tokens, 30 That the wicked is reserved to the day of destruction? they shall be brought forth to the day of wrath. 31 Who shall declare his way to his face? and who shall repay him what he hath done? 32 Yet shall he be brought to the grave, and shall remain in the tomb. 33 The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him, and every man shall draw after him, as there are innumerable before him. 34 How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing in your answers there remaineth falsehood?

21.26.1.en: Behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me [27].

21.26.2.en: Job turns again to rebuke his friends, telling them that he knows that they hold fast to their opinions, especially that the wicked are surely pursued by calamities. Job says to his friends: I have known that you do not agree with me, and I have known your intention toward me, for you are prejudiced against me; how then can I persuade you when you are biased? Job perceived through their words what was in their hearts, and felt that dialogue with them was fruitless.

21.26.3.en: * "Behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me" [27]. As it is written: "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?" (1 Cor 2:11)... But the spirit of man is unknown to others unless it appears in words or deeds. It is written: "By their fruits ye shall know them" (Mt 7:20). By what happens outside, what is hidden within is seen. So also it was rightly said of Solomon: [As faces shine in water, so the hearts of men are clear to the wise] (Prov 27:19)...

21.26.5.en: For ye say, Where is the house of the prince?

21.27.0.en: and where are the dwelling places of the wicked? [28]

21.27.1.en: As though he says to them: I know that you will answer me saying: Where is the house of the usurper? Where is the tent of the wicked? And you mean me by the usurper as you mean my sons by the wicked. You judge me to be a tyrant, and my children wicked.

21.27.2.en: If we remove the evil intention of Job's friends, and their desperate attempt to distort his character, then what they say does apply to ruthless tyrants and usurpers. For though they live all their days in wealth, honor and authority, they die and return to their dust. Then it is rightly said: "Where is the house of the prince?" He who thinks that the whole world is his settled house, which he controls and governs as the master of a house who lives in it forever, and none can drive him out or pull down the house. Tyrants through the generations died who counted themselves gods, but they became dust, and their kingdoms were utterly overthrown. In folly they lived in the world as in unstable tents, and behold, the tents have vanished and their authority has vanished with them.

21.27.3.en: * It is said of the wicked after their death: "Where are the dwelling places of the wicked?" If we look closely at this, can you deny that there is recompense from divine justice? The first (the righteous) has happiness flooding his heart, and the second misery. The first by the witness of his own soul is innocent of guilt, and the second a criminal. That man is happy in his departure from the world, and the second is sorrowful over it. Who can pronounce innocence on one who is not innocent in the eyes of his own conscience? He says: [Where is the covering of his tent, his memorial shall not be found] (cf. Job 21:28). The life of the criminal is a dream. No, even the very rest of the wicked while they live here is an illusion; they are now in hell, for they go down to Gehenna while still alive.

21.27.4.en: St. Ambrose * The weak desire success in the wealth of the world, and fear blows as though they were exceedingly grave evils, and they stumble at the punishment of those whom they see struck.

21.28.0.en: "Have ye not asked them that go by the way? and do ye not know their tokens?" [29]

21.29.0.en: That the wicked is reserved to the day of destruction? they shall be brought forth to the day of wrath. [30]

21.29.1.en: Job knows that dialogue is futile with people who do not bear a sincere and honest intention, so he asks them to question any neutral person. Ask those who pass by the road, whoever they may be.

21.29.2.en: He did not say ask the saints as Eliphaz said (Job 5:1), for the matter does not even need the experiences of the saints, but is known to every unbiased person, since all humanity agrees with Job that sinners do not necessarily receive their recompense here, but it may be deferred to the great day of the Lord. [When the wicked flourish, it is that they shall be destroyed for ever] (Ps 92:7).

21.29.3.en: Perhaps by his calling them to ask any passerby he means that they should look for anyone who perceives the truth of this temporal life as a passing road, for such a man will surely speak the truth, with wisdom and sincerity. A man's perceiving the truth of his life, that it is a passing as over a bridge, gives him a realistic view of temporal life and the eternal life to come, so his judgment of matters is balanced and true!

21.29.4.en: *He calls [one who passes by the way] him who holds in his mind that the present life is for him a road and not a homeland. He counts it a base thing for him to fix his heart in love of the present passing state, longing not to remain occupied with viewing temporal things, but to reach with his heart the eternal world...

21.29.5.en: When Moses sought the glory of heavenly contemplation he said: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight" (Ex 3:3). For unless he withdraws the traces of his feet from the love of the world he cannot understand the things above.

21.29.6.en: When Jeremiah besought that the sorrow of his heart be considered he said: "All ye that pass by the way, behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow" (Lam 1:12). For those who do not pass through the present life as through a road, but think it their homeland, have no experience to see with the eyes of the mind the sorrow of the heart of the elect. Does the prophet look to them that they may see his sorrow?

21.30.0.en: Who shall declare his way to his face? and who shall repay him what he hath done? [31]

21.30.1.en: The wicked man bears a kind of boldness and might, so he finds none to stand before him and confront him with his wickedness, nor anyone to punish him for his deeds. He sins and plunders while secure. No one rebukes him or terrifies him. The wise man says: [the prosperity of fools shall destroy them] (Prov 1:22), as they count themselves above the law, with none able to confront them with their wickedness, or to move them toward repentance and return to the true God.

21.30.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) noted that Job turned his speech about the wicked from the plural form to the singular. He sees in the plural (the wicked) a reference to human beings who have become like many members of the body of the devil, and in the singular (the wicked man) a reference to the devil as the head of the wicked. As believers are members of the body of Christ, the holy Head, so the wicked are members of the body of the devil, the evil head!

21.30.3.en: * "Who will denounce his way to his face? and who will repay him for his work?" [31]... While Job was speaking of all the wicked, suddenly he turned his words to the head of all the wicked. For he saw, at the end of the world, Satan entering into a man, whom Holy Scripture calls "the antichrist," who exalts himself proudly, supported by such authority as to be lifted up with signs and wonders displaying a (deceptive) holiness, and who cannot be accused by any man. By the authority of terror he unites the signs of outward holiness. He says: "Who will denounce his way to his face?" meaning, who of mankind dares and rebukes him...? But Elijah and Enoch alone will be present at once to rebuke him. Then all the elect will rebuke his way to his face, showing contempt; and while he is proud in thought they resist his evil. And since they do this by divine grace and not by their own strength, it is rightly said now: "Who will denounce his way to his face?" Who does this but God, by whose help the elect receive authority to stand before him? For the Lord alone can do that by His power. Rightly it is said of him: [Whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming] (2 Thess 2:8)...

21.30.4.en: [Who will repay him for his work?] Truly who but the Lord, who alone will repay that perishing man for what he does with eternal judgment?

21.31.0.en: Yet shall he be brought to the grave, and shall remain in the tomb [32].

21.31.1.en: The wicked man knows that he will surely die like the rest of men, but he prepares greatness for himself even in his death, so he sets up a memorial monument over the grave he prepares for himself, and arranges a splendid funeral procession for himself.

21.31.2.en: While many of the wicked care for temporal honor even after their passing from this world, caring for their bodies after death or the tomb or the erection of a memorial to them, the righteous are occupied with nothing but meeting the heavenly Bridegroom. They long to depart to be with Christ, which is better for them than every work however valuable.

21.31.3.en: * "He shall be brought to the graves, and shall keep watch over the heap of dead bodies" [32]... There are few righteous in the world and a multitude of the wicked. Therefore it is rightly said: "heap of dead bodies," as it points to the multitude of the wicked. "Because wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat" (Mt 7:13). Thus Satan keeps watch over the heap of dead bodies, practicing the deceits of his wickedness in the hearts of the sons of perdition.

21.31.5.en: The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him (the mud of the valley).

21.32.0.en: and every man shall draw after him, as there are innumerable before him [33].

21.32.1.en: As he refers to the antichrist as the representative of the evil devil, who sets himself up as God in the temple of the Lord, Job sees him as nothing but a mortal man who becomes dust and ashes.

21.32.2.en: By his saying [the clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him], Job sees that his death and return to dust is better for him than his life, because he usurps divine glory, and counts himself immortal, and leads a movement of rebellion and persecution against the Church of the Lord Christ.

21.32.3.en: Perhaps he points here to the wicked man's preparing everything for the embalming of his body and the pouring of spices on his corpse though he has nothing but the clods of the valley in which he is buried. He takes no warning from death, and does not remember that he is not the only one who faces death, but countless numbers have preceded him, and every man will come after him; all die without exception.

21.32.4.en: * "He draws every man after him, and there are innumerable before him" [33]. In this place the word "man" means one who tastes human things... Our ancient enemy, entering the man of perdition, draws all the carnal whom he finds under the yoke of his authority.

21.33.0.en: How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing in your answers there remaineth falsehood? [34].

21.33.1.en: Job ends his speech by returning to the plural form, that is, to speaking with the wicked. What befalls the wicked of destruction and ruin will not exempt them from judgment.

21.33.2.en: If the wicked claim to desire to comfort the suffering, their consolation is vain.

21.33.3.en: Job rejects their dialogue and their arguments because they come from insincere hearts, but carry a spirit of betrayal of friendship, and because their claims are vain, as they concentrate on his repentance so that he might enjoy returning to the state of prosperity he was in before the calamities came.

21.33.4.en: There is no room for consolation when it comes from hearts that bear no love!

21.33.5.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the dialogue of these friends caused him pains, and instead of binding up his wounds the wounds increased. On one side the righteous man suffers from their lack of faithfulness and sincerity, not because of the accusations in themselves, but because of their insincerity and the betrayal of the friendship that existed between him and them.

21.33.6.en: His soul suffers and is embittered, because he is a lover of the truth and desires the salvation of all, and finds the odor of the sin of death rising from their depths. His soul groans over their destruction more than his bitterness over the accusations directed against him!

21.33.7.en: * "How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing your answers show that they are against the truth" [34]. Job's friends were not able to comfort him, they who in their dialogue oppose the truth. When they called him a hypocrite or wicked they committed the crime of the sin of lying, and surely added troubles to the righteous man, and to his wounds. For the minds of the saints, being subject to the truth, suffer because of the sins of deceiving others. As much as they strongly perceive that the crime of falsehood is grave, they hate it not only if they commit it but also if others commit it.

21.33.9.en: My soul trembles at the destruction of the wicked!

21.33.10.en: * Many are occupied with asking: Why does God prosper the way of the wicked?

21.33.11.en: But what occupies me is their eternity!

21.33.12.en: Yes, the wicked may prosper and flourish, they may enjoy positions of power!

21.33.13.en: They think they are secure, and that they are above every law!

21.33.14.en: All that is around them gives them reassurance and peace.

21.33.15.en: * My soul grieves not at their success, but because they insult God's longsuffering and forbearance.

21.33.16.en: They count worship a waste of their time and energies.

21.33.17.en: Their life is not in the hand of the Almighty.

21.33.18.en: But I see their lamp suddenly go out.

21.33.19.en: * My heart groans as it sees them like stubble before the wind, and like chaff in the midst of a whirlwind!

21.33.20.en: Their days pass like a passing moment, their tents collapse completely.

21.33.21.en: * I wonder how they will stand before the judgment seat?

21.33.22.en: Wretched are those who have lost the glory!

21.33.23.en: They ask the mountains to fall on them, and the hills to cover them!

21.33.24.en: With Jeremiah the prophet I cry:

21.33.25.en: The walls of my heart pain me!

21.33.26.en: It is melted like wax within me.

21.33.27.en: My evils give me a momentary pleasure, accompanied by destruction of my whole being.
